If that liquid phase is water, fluxes are limited by the driving force since CO is present on both sides of the membrane. 2 Transformation of algae to increase carbon uptake Algae have evolved Carbon Concentrating Mechanisms (CCMs) to increase the rate of delivery of CO to the first steps of carbon fixation (Giordano et al. 2005). CCMs 2 are induced in ambient CO conditions and knocking out particular components 2 leads to low rates of photosynthesis or even death unless cells are grown in high (up to 5%) CO (Takashi and Hideya, 2009). Thus far, the only genetically proven 2 component of N. oceanica’s CCM are carbonic anhydrases which interchange CO 2 and HCO -. Both Nannochloropsis salina and N. gaditana appear to have a 3 bicarbonate pump for CO whereby bicarbonate is actively transported across the 2 plasma membrane and then presumably converted to CO by intracellular carbonic 2 anhydrases (Hanson et al., 2014). There have not been any reports of expression of cyanobacterial bicarbonate transporters into a (eukoryotic) alga. CO transfer technologies for algal cultivations 2 Transferring CO efficiently into algae cultivations is a critical process for optimizing 2 6 algal growth and maximizing biomass production, especially for biofuel applications. The standard method involves direct bubbling (sparging) of CO or a CO -enriched 2 2 air or waste gas mixture directly into algal culture systems. This approach can be easily implemented in both open pond systems and closed photobioreactors, using spargers that distribute gas bubbles evenly through the liquid medium. The key to this process is optimizing the bubble size and residence time within the medium, as these factors significantly influence the dissolution rate of CO and its uptake by the 2 algae. Recent studies suggest that microbubbles, due to their high surface area to volume ratio, can enhance CO transfer efficiency, providing a more effective and 2 economically viable solution compared to larger bubbles (Yang et al., 2018). An alternative approach involves the use of membrane contactors, which facilitate CO transfer across a semi-permeable membrane into the algal cultivation system. 2 This method allows for precise control over CO delivery rates and prevents gas 2 losses to the atmosphere, making it particularly advantageous in closed systems. By maintaining a stable carbon supply, membrane contactors can significantly improve algal growth rates and biomass productivity. Recent advancements in membrane technology have focused on improving the durability and permeability of these contactors to withstand prolonged operational periods, potentially reducing operational costs and increasing the sustainability of large-scale algae cultivation (Bilad et al. 2014). 6. The project contributed to the technical effectiveness and economic feasibility of algal cultivations primarily through development of the membrane system for CO 2 delivery with much improved CUE.
